content.text: Asia-Pacific leads global progress on energy access, but key gaps remain

Electrification improved by nearly 380 million people, raising the regional access rate from 94% in 2016 to 99% in 2021. Global energy access progress was largely driven by significant progress in Asia, especially India and Bangladesh. In Central and Southern Asia, the number without access fell dramatically from 414 million in 2010 to 24 million in 2021, while Eastern and South-eastern Asia saw a decline from 90 million to 35 million. Despite this progress, Myanmar, Pakistan, and North Korea still have about 40 million people without electricity. Additionally, around 50 million people, mainly in rural low-income areas, still lack reliable electricity, highlighting the need for focused policies on last-mile access and quality. If efforts do not increase, an estimated 660 million people—560 million in Sub-Saharan Africa and 70 million in Developing Asia—will remain unserved by 2030.

Between 2010 and 2021, access to clean cooking improved from 51% to 74%, yet around 1.2 billion people—especially in rural areas and Small Island Developing States (SIDS)—still lack it due to challenges like technology, cultural preferences, affordability, and low investment. Clean cooking significantly benefits health by reducing indoor air pollution, mainly affecting women and children, and lessens women’s time poverty by easing firewood collection and improving cooking efficiency. Adoption of clean cooking also positively impacts girls’ school attendance. To advance clean cooking, integrating social policies and employment strategies into regional energy plans is vital. Affordability can be boosted through targeted subsidies and microfinance, with cleaner fuels like LPG offering practical rural solutions. Programs in India, Indonesia, and Bhutan are driving transitions from traditional to cleaner cooking methods, including India’s LPG subsidies specifically targeting female-headed households and promoting women’s financial inclusion.

content.title: Key Concepts
content.intro: Explore foundational ideas from this lesson.

concepts.title: grid reliability
concepts.body: Grid reliability refers to the ability of an electrical grid to consistently deliver electricity to consumers without interruptions or failures.

concepts.title: low-carbon transport
concepts.body: Low-carbon transport refers to transportation methods and systems that produce minimal greenhouse gas emissions, often through the use of renewable energy sources, electric vehicles, public transit, cycling, and walking.

concepts.title: sustainable heating
concepts.body: Sustainable heating refers to methods of heating spaces that minimize environmental impact, often using renewable energy sources, energy efficiency practices, and low-carbon technologies.

content.text: Coal dominates electricity generation

Coal dominates electricity generation in the region, accounting for 58% of the total share, and power generation (electricity and heat) is responsible for 53% of CO2 emissions, mostly from coal. This underscores the urgent need for decarbonization efforts focused on shifting from coal to cleaner, renewable sources like solar, wind, and hydropower. While fossil fuels such as coal and oil currently drive economic growth and motorization, renewable energy adoption remains low. Although gas grids are expanding, the future role of natural gas is uncertain, posing challenges for fossil-fuel-dependent economies that face fiscal vulnerabilities. These countries require both international support and domestic reforms to navigate global decarbonization pressures.
1 in 3 people struggle to afford energy

Despite being home to the world’s largest hydrocarbon exporters, the RBEC region faces significant energy poverty, with about one in three people struggling to afford energy amid aging infrastructure and frequent power cuts in harsh winters. Electrification is nearly universal, estimated at close to 100%, but outdated systems require urgent modernization. The recent energy crisis and conflicts have worsened the situation— for example, in Moldova, 71% of households spend 90% or more of their disposable income on energy and heating during cold periods. This forces many to switch to cheaper but environmentally harmful heating options, highlighting the urgent need to address energy affordability and improve living conditions.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation

content.text: Lesson 2 Overview

Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) stand at a pivotal crossroads. The region is endowed with some of the richest renewable energy resources in the world – abundant solar in Mexico and Chile, strong winds in Patagonia, expansive hydro resources in Brazil and the Andes, and emerging geothermal and green hydrogen opportunities. At the same time, it grapples with persistent inequality, energy poverty, climate vulnerability, and slow investment flows.

This lesson explores how the region’s vast energy potential can be harnessed to drive inclusive and sustainable development. Energy is not just a sector – it is an enabler. It powers schools and clinics, fuels jobs and industrial growth, supports digital inclusion, and provides resilience against disasters and shocks. Yet, 17 million people still lack access to electricity, and 78 million rely on traditional fuels for cooking – exposing deep energy access gaps that must be addressed if the region is to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Despite having one of the cleanest electricity mixes globally (over 60% renewable), LAC remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels for transport and industry. The challenge now is twofold: ensuring universal access to modern energy and shifting energy systems toward resilience, equity, and sustainability.

By combining regional data, policy analysis, and forward-looking opportunities, learners will gain a holistic view of why sustainable energy is a cornerstone for economic transformation, climate action, and social justice across Latin America and the Caribbean.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: A: Development Context in Latin America and the Caribbean

content.text:
Latin America and the Caribbean is a region marked by both rich natural resources and persistent development challenges. While it boasts one of the cleanest electricity matrices globally – 41% hydropower, 8% wind, 6.2% solar – this green advantage coexists with structural inequalities, fiscal constraints, and energy poverty.

LAC remains one of the most unequal regions globally. Countries like Brazil, Chile, and Mexico have some of the highest inequality rates in the world.

Approximately 80% of the population live in urban areas, and the region faces unique vulnerability to natural disasters and climate shocks – 152 million people were affected by 1,205 natural disasters between 2000 and 2019. At the same time, the region holds exceptional potential in hydropower, solar, and wind, presenting a rare opportunity to leapfrog into a clean and just energy future.

still lack access to clean cooking and around 17 million people lack access to electricity, primarily in rural and remote areas.

The region's renewable energy potential, combined with smart finance, inclusive policies, and industrial innovation can transform these vulnerabilities into engines for inclusive growth and climate resilience.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: B: Energy Challenges in Latin America and the Caribbean

content.text:
The region has achieved a high electricity access rate of 97.6% as of 2021, but these gains are uneven.

17 million people, mostly in rural and Indigenous communities, remain unelectrified. In Haiti, for instance, only 47% of people have electricity access, and just 5% have access to clean cooking solutions.

Access is not just about lighting homes – it's about enabling education, health care, livelihoods, and climate adaptation. Last-mile electrification strategies, decentralized renewable systems, and digital tools (e.g., pay-as-you-go solar) present immediate and scalable solutions.

78 million people lack access to clean cooking, severely impacting health and disproportionately burdening women and girls.

Development Opportunity: Expanding energy access improves education, health, productivity, and gender equality. In rural areas, modern energy solutions reduce women's time poverty and improve economic opportunities. Solar mini-grids, digital pay-as-you-go models, and off-grid solutions are transforming energy access across Central America and the Caribbean.

LAC is uniquely positioned for a low-carbon transition. Renewable energy investments have soared, with solar and wind driving new capacity installations. However, fossil fuels still account for 66% of primary energy supply in the entire region and over 90% in the Caribbean.

Scaling renewables is not only about decarbonization for he region – it's an engine for job creation and industrial transformation. The region could generate millions of green jobs if policy, finance, and local innovation are aligned. ECLAC estimates that 1.33% of GDP annually from 2021-2032 could make energy sources 86% renewable and cut GHG emissions by 30%.

Additionally,

In Energy Efficiency: Despite a 17% drop in energy intensity over 30 years, efficiency gains are slow. The building and transport sectors are ripe for scalable improvements.
In Green Hydrogen Potential: With low-cost renewables, LAC can become a global green hydrogen hub. Countries like Chile, Brazil, and Uruguay are leading with over 25 pilot projects under development.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: C: Energy Opportunities in Latin America and the Caribbean

content.text:
Finance is the linchpin of the transition. Global clean energy investments reached $1.3 trillion in 2022, yet only a fraction flows to LAC. To meet energy access and SDG 7 goals, LAC requires significant upscaling of finance ranging $125–200 billion annually across renewables, efficiency, access, and resilience.

Innovative blended finance, green bonds, and concessional loans are crucial to attract private investment. Strategic use of public funds (e.g., GEF, GCF) to de-risk private capital is key and should be seriously considered, and national development banks are pivotal in structuring financial tools

Properly structured finance can drive localized development – empowering communities, boosting productivity, and promoting climate-smart agriculture, e-mobility, and circular economies.
Fossil Fuel Use is still dominant

It should not be a surprise that natural gas and oil are still the largest sources of energy, given the concentration of producers in the region. Electricity generation in the Arab States is fueled mostly by natural gas at 72% followed by oil at 25%. With a heavy dependence on fossil fuels, electricity and heat generation were responsible for 39% of total carbon emissions in the region. In contrast, only 7% of power flows from renewable energy.
Need for Increasing Renewables Capacity

The region lags others in terms of renewable energy production. However, there is promise to be found in the region’s increasing capacity for renewables, which has multiplied tenfold over the past decade.

content.title: The total installed renewable energy capacity is at 23.6 GW, with 5.1 GW added from just 2018 to 2020.
content.body: The capacity increase has been concentrated in a few countries, such as Egypt, Jordan, and Morocco. It also has been mostly for PV, with capacity more than doubling from 3.2 GW in 2018 to 7.4 GW by the end of 2020. Wind energy and CSP saw only minor increases. Perhaps unexpectedly, oil-producing countries have also increasingly turned to solar to supply local electricity, with several mega-scale projects under development. This is part of efforts to conserve oil and gas reserves for future export revenues.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: D: Energy Strategy for the Region

content.text: 4 key areas of priority have been identified for the region

a. Closing the Energy Access Gap
Enhancing energy access is directly linked to reducing multidimensional poverty. Households with energy access experience improved educational outcomes, health, and productivity.
Digital payment models (e.g., pay-as-you-go solar) and community-led electrification are scalable across off-grid and rural areas.

b. Accelerating a Just Energy Transition
Transitioning to renewables could cut emissions by 30% and make the energy mix 86% renewable by 2032 with just 1.33% of GDP annual investment.
It also creates gender-responsive employment opportunities and reduces inequality if designed inclusively.

c. Strengthening Energy Resilience
Caribbean states spend up to 1.2% of GDP on natural disaster recovery annually. Resilient infrastructure – especially solar mini-grids – can protect critical services during disasters.

d. Driving Energy Finance and Investment
Only 1.3% of regional GDP goes to fossil fuel subsidies, a significant fiscal burden. Redirecting subsidies to clean investments could generate better returns, equity, and environmental benefits.
Regional development banks and local financial institutions (with nearly $1 trillion in assets) are crucial for unlocking blended finance and de-risking projects.
Financing is critical
Globally, clean energy investments reached $1.3 trillion in 2022, but only a small share goes to Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), which needs $125–200 billion annually to meet SDG 7 targets.

Innovative tools like blended finance, green bonds, and concessional loans—backed by public funding through mechanisms such as the GEF and GCF—are vital to mobilize private capital. National development banks also play a crucial role. Well-structured finance can catalyze inclusive development by supporting energy access, productivity, e-mobility, climate-resilient agriculture, and circular economies.
